title: Pig — the dice push
players: 2–4 players (or one big group taking turns)
equipment: 1 die (or write 1–6 on six pieces of paper, fold them, draw from a cup)
paper to track scores
a pen
intro: Pig is one of the simplest gambling games ever made. You'll feel the texture of risk-and-reward in five minutes. Every roll is a small choice: keep what you have, or push for more.

steps.title: Set up
steps.body: Two players sit facing each other with a die between them. Each player has a score that starts at 0.
steps.svg:
<svg viewBox='0 0 200 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'>
<g transform='translate(50,60)'><circle cx='0' cy='-15' r='8' fill='#2D3127'/>
<line x1='0' y1='-7' x2='0' y2='15' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/>
<line x1='-12' y1='0' x2='12' y2='0' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/>
<line x1='0' y1='15' x2='-8' y2='30' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/>

steps.title: Roll
steps.body: On your turn, roll the die. Whatever you roll (2–6) is added to a temporary 'turn score' — not yet your real score.
steps.svg:
<svg viewBox='0 0 60 60' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'>
<rect x='10' y='10' width='40' height='40' rx='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='2'/>

<circle cx='40' cy='40' r='3' fill='#2D3127'/></svg>

steps.title: Bank or push?
steps.body: After each roll: BANK (add turn score to real score, end turn) or PUSH (roll again, risking everything).
steps.svg:
<svg viewBox='0 0 100 80' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'>
<rect x='15' y='25' width='70' height='40' fill='#FFF1EA' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='2' rx='3'/>
<text x='50' y='52' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Fraunces' font-size='18' font-weight='600' fill='#C75B39'>+12</text>
<text x='50' y='75' text-anchor='middle' font-family='IBM Plex Mono' font-size='9' fill='#6B6960' letter-spacing='0.1em'>BANKED</text></svg>

steps.title: Push
steps.body: If you push, you roll again. As long as you don't roll a 1, you can keep pushing.
steps.svg:
<svg viewBox='0 0 100 80' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'>
<rect x='15' y='25' width='70' height='40' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='2' rx='3' stroke-dasharray='4,3'/>
<text x='50' y='52' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Fraunces' font-size='18' font-weight='600' fill='#2D3127'>+?</text>
<text x='50' y='75' text-anchor='middle' font-family='IBM Plex Mono' font-size='9' fill='#6B6960' letter-spacing='0.1em'>ROLL AGAIN</text></svg>

steps.title: Bust
steps.body: If you ever roll a 1, you BUST. Your turn score evaporates. Your turn ends.
steps.svg:
<svg viewBox='0 0 60 60' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'>
<rect x='10' y='10' width='40' height='40' rx='5' fill='#FFE5DC' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='2'/>
<circle cx='30' cy='30' r='4' fill='#C75B39'/>
<text x='30' y='58' text-anchor='middle' font-family='IBM Plex Mono' font-size='8' fill='#C75B39'>BUST</text></svg>

steps.title: Goal
steps.body: The first player to bank 20 points wins. Play three games.
steps.svg:
<svg viewBox='0 0 100 80' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'>
<rect x='25' y='15' width='50' height='50' fill='#FFE5DC' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='2.5' rx='4'/>
<text x='50' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Fraunces' font-size='20' font-weight='600' fill='#C75B39'>30</text>

<g transform='translate(50,73)'>
<path d='M -8 -3 L 0 4 L 8 -3' fill='none' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='2' stroke-linecap='round'/>
</g></svg>

what_to_notice: Did pushing feel exciting or frustrating?

animation.narration: Two players. First to bank 20 points wins.
Player 1 rolls a 4. Turn score = 4.
Pushes. Rolls 5. Turn score = 9.
Pushes again. Rolls 1. BUST — loses all 9.
Player 2 rolls a 5. Pushes. Rolls 3. Turn = 8.
Player 2 banks. Plays it safe. Total = 8.
Player 1 rolls 6, then 4. Banks 10. Total = 10.
Player 2 pushes hard — banks 12. Total = 20. Wins.

questions.question: What happens when a player rolls a 1 in this game?
options: They lose all the points they had built up this turn.
questions.feedback_correct: Right. The 1 is the BUST — everything in your turn-score is lost.
questions.feedback_wrong: Look again — when a 1 is rolled, the player loses all the points they built up that turn.

questions.question: Why did Player 2 bank early when their turn-score was just 8?
options: They had no choice: the rules forced it.
They were far ahead, so they could play safe.
They had just watched Player 1 lose 9 points by pushing, so 8 sure points felt safer.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Banking chooses a sure 8 over the chance of more.
questions.feedback_wrong: Player 2 had just watched Player 1 push and lose all 9 points. Banking keeps 8 for certain.

questions.question: What kind of game-design mechanic is this?
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Push-your-luck is the family. Every roll is a 'one more?' decision.
questions.feedback_wrong: The defining feature is the choice to keep going for more reward, with the risk of losing everything.

questions.question: If you wanted players to feel TENSE, which change would you try?
options: Make the bust cost bigger (lose all points ever banked).
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. A bigger loss on a bust raises the stakes; removing the bank removes the choice. Talk about which you would try, and what it would change.

title: Three-card Hanabi — hidden hands and clues
equipment: 12 small paper cards — write numbers 1–4 in three colours (red, blue, green). 4 cards per colour.
a paper to track which cards have been played
intro: In Hanabi you can see everyone's cards except your own. You hold your cards facing outward: your teammates see them, and you work out yours from their clues.

steps.title: Make the cards
steps.body: On 12 small paper cards, write red 1–4, blue 1–4, green 1–4.

what_to_notice: Did the restriction feel like a problem or like the point?

animation.narration: Three players. Cards face outward — you see others' cards, not your own.
P1 says: 'You have one red.' That's a clue to P2 about colour only.
P2 thinks: 'one of my cards is red — but which?'
P2 plays the second card — guesses it's red 1. Right!
P3 plays a card — guesses red. But it was blue 2. Lose a life.
P1 gives clue: 'two reds in your hand' — but only to P3.
The cards run out. The team has played four cards in order and kept two lives.

questions.question: Why do players hold their cards facing outward?
options: So their teammates can see what they hold but they can't see their own.
So the dealer can keep score.
Because the cards are too big to hold normally.
Because Hanabi is a betting game.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The asymmetry of information — others see you, you don't see yourself — is the heart of the game.
questions.feedback_wrong: It's about asymmetry — teammates see your cards but you don't see them. Information is the puzzle.

questions.question: What's a clue you ARE allowed to give in this game?
options: 'Play the second card from your left.'
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Clues name only one feature — colour or number — never strategy or specific instructions.
questions.feedback_wrong: Clues name ONE feature only — a colour or a number. They never tell someone what to do.

questions.question: What kind of game-design mechanic is this?
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The team plays together, and the constraint on talking is what makes it a game.
questions.feedback_wrong: Players cooperate, but the rules limit what they can say. The constraint IS the puzzle.

questions.question: If you wanted players to feel CLEVER, which change would you try?
options: Limit clues to one feature only — they have to read between the lines.
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. Clues limited to one feature leave players to work out the rest; open talk removes that. Talk about which you would try.

title: The blocking grid — workers fight for spots
parent_game: Simplified worker placement (like in Stone Age)
equipment: a sheet of paper
a pen
four small objects per player, different for each player (coins, eraser bits, paper clips)

what_to_notice: Did blocking feel mean or fun?
When did you predict opponent's move?
Was the choice — high spot or save tokens — interesting?

animation.narration: Two players. 3×3 grid of spots. Each spot scores 3, 2, or 1 points.
P1 takes the top-left 3-point WOOD spot.
P2 takes the top-centre 3-point STONE spot.
P1 takes the top-right 3-point GOLD. All top spots gone.
P2 plays middle WOOD — settles for 2 since 3-row is full.
P1 takes middle STONE — 2 more points.
P2 takes middle GOLD. P1 plays bottom WOOD, P2 bottom STONE. Final: P1 9, P2 8.

questions.question: What happens when a player places a token on a spot?
options: The other player gets to place there too.
The spot is blocked — no one else can use it this round.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Blocking is the core. Once a spot is taken, the other player has to choose elsewhere.
questions.feedback_wrong: The whole point is that taking a spot blocks it — the other player has to pick something else.

questions.question: Why did P2 play the middle WOOD spot for 2 points instead of going for the 3-point row?
options: All the 3-point spots were blocked already.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Blocking shapes choice. P2 had to pick from what wasn't taken.
questions.feedback_wrong: All three top-row 3-point spots were already blocked. P2 had to pick from the remaining options.

questions.question: What kind of game-design mechanic is this?
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Worker placement: each spot taken is a spot blocked.
questions.feedback_wrong: This is the classic worker-placement pattern — taking a spot denies it to others.

questions.question: If you wanted to make this game LESS confrontational, which change would you try?
options: Allow multiple players on one spot (no blocking).
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. Letting players share a spot removes the blocking, and with it most of the contest for spots. Talk about what the game would become.

questions.question: Why is 5×5 four-in-a-row more interesting than regular 3×3 tic-tac-toe?
options: With more space, you can plan multiple threats — strategy opens up.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. With more space, each player can build more than one threat at a time.
questions.feedback_wrong: More space lets a player build two threats at once, and the other player can block only one.

questions.question: What's the most important skill in this game?
options: Reading your opponent's plan and blocking it before it completes.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The whole game is about seeing threats and choosing whether to block or build.
questions.feedback_wrong: It's about reading. You watch what your opponent is building and decide: block, or build your own threat?

questions.question: What kind of game-design mechanic is this?
options: Pattern building (you're trying to make a specific shape)
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The game is about building a specific pattern (4-in-a-row) before your opponent.
questions.feedback_wrong: You're racing to create a specific arrangement of marks. That's pattern-building.

questions.question: If you wanted players to feel THOUGHTFUL, which change would you try?
options: Make the grid larger so multi-step plans become possible.
Use random tokens instead of choosing.
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. A larger grid leaves room for longer plans; a timer cuts them short. Talk about which you would try.

questions.question: Why does memory matter in this game?
options: Cards stay face-down except briefly during flips. Remembering what you saw earlier helps you find pairs.
The rules require a memory test before playing.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Cards revealed once go back face-down — but the information is still in your head, if you remember.
questions.feedback_wrong: Cards flip face-up briefly, then go back. The information you saw is still useful — if you remembered it.

questions.question: What kind of game-design mechanic is this?
options: Set collection — you collect matching pairs.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. You collect matching pairs — that's set-collection.
questions.feedback_wrong: You're collecting matching pairs. That's set-collection — gathering completed sets to score.

questions.question: After a few turns, what happens to the role of luck?
options: As more cards have been seen, skill (memory) starts to matter more than luck.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Early flips are blind. As more cards are revealed, the decisions become memory-driven.
questions.feedback_wrong: Early flips are blind. As more cards are seen, memory takes over from luck.

questions.question: If you wanted to make this game require more SKILL and less LUCK, what would you change?
options: Show cards for longer when flipped.
Hide them faster — give players less time to memorise.
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. More pairs give memory more to hold; showing cards for longer makes remembering easier. Talk about what each would change.

animation.narration: Five players sit in a circle. One is the wolf. Nobody knows who.
Day. Players talk. P1 says: 'P3 hasn't said anything.' Others nod.
P3 (the wolf) defends: 'I'm just listening — like always.'
Vote. P1, P2, P5 vote P3. P3 is OUT — and revealed as the wolf!

questions.question: What makes this game different from a normal cooperative game?
options: Players are all on the same side.
One player has a secret goal opposed to the others — the others have to deduce who it is.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The hidden adversary is the engine — most players cooperate, one works against them in secret.
questions.feedback_wrong: There's a hidden adversary. Most players are on one team, one is secretly on another. The cooperation is partial.

questions.question: If you were the wolf, how would you play?
options: Talk normally — neither too quiet nor too eager. Deflect suspicion onto others.
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. Some wolves stay quiet, some talk a lot, some accuse others. Talk about what you saw P3 do, and what you would try.

questions.question: What kind of game-design mechanic is this?
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Hidden identity, deduction, and the traitor pattern all live in this family.
questions.feedback_wrong: This is the social-deduction family — a hidden traitor, the rest deducing who it is.

questions.question: If you wanted players to feel TENSE, which change would you try?
options: Make the wolf's elimination final and immediate (no second chances).
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. Final eliminations make each accusation weigh more; showing every role ends the game. Talk about which you would try.

title: Paper auction — bid for the prize

equipment: 30 small paper bits per player (their bidding tokens)

intro: Auctions are deceptively simple games of value. Pay too much for a prize and you've won the wrong way. Pay too little and you walk away empty-handed.

animation.narration: Three players. Each starts with 30 tokens. Five prizes in the bag.
First prize: a 5. The biggest one. Players bid secretly.
P3 wins with 18 tokens. Pays 18. Takes the 5-prize.
Next prize: a 3. P3 has fewer tokens. P1 wins with 11.
Three more rounds. P3 has only 12 tokens left, and P1 outbids them for the 4. P2 takes the 2, P3 the 1. Final prize values: P1 7, P2 2, P3 6. P1 wins.

questions.question: What's the central tension in this game?
options: Bidding too much wastes tokens; bidding too little loses the prize.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Every bid is a balance — pay enough to win, but not so much you lose value.
questions.feedback_wrong: It's about balance. Bid too high and you waste tokens; bid too low and you lose the prize.

questions.question: Why is it risky to spend a lot on the first prize?
options: If you spend big early, you have less for later — and can't win when the biggest prize comes.
First prizes are always low value.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Tokens spent are gone. Big early spending leaves you short for later rounds.
questions.feedback_wrong: Tokens are finite. Spending a lot early means you'll be outbid on later prizes.

questions.question: What kind of game-design mechanic is this?
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The whole game runs on bidding.
questions.feedback_wrong: This is the bidding family — players spend resources to win the right to take an action.

questions.question: If you wanted players to feel CLEVER, which change would you try?
options: Show all bids openly so others can see who's bidding what.
Keep bids secret and reveal simultaneously — players have to guess what others will do.
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. Secret bids make players guess each other; open bids let them react. Talk about which you would try.

title: Pick-and-pass — the drafting game
equipment: 24 small paper cards — write each card with a colour and a number (4 colours × 6 numbers per colour)
a flat surface to lay cards
intro: Drafting is a compact, satisfying game pattern. You see a small set of cards, pick the one that helps your plan, pass the rest. Others get what you didn't take.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'draft' a card in this game?
options: Pick one card from your hand, pass the rest.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Drafting = pick one, pass the rest. The cards rotate around the table.
questions.feedback_wrong: To draft is to pick one card from your hand and pass the rest to the next player. The hand rotates.

questions.question: Why might you keep a card you don't want?
options: You can't — you must keep useful ones.
To prevent another player from getting it.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Denying a card to your opponent is part of drafting. You can take a card just to prevent them from having it.
questions.feedback_wrong: You can take a card to deny it to others. 'Hate-drafting' is a real strategy.

questions.question: What kind of game-design mechanic is this?
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Drafting is the family — pick from a shared pool, pass the rest.
questions.feedback_wrong: Drafting: pick from a rotating hand, pass the rest.

questions.question: If you wanted players to feel THOUGHTFUL, which change would you try?
options: Show every player's collection so everyone sees what each is going for.
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. Showing each player's collection lets others read their plans; a timer leaves less time to think. Talk about which you would try.

intro: UNO works because the rule is so simple: get rid of all your cards. The whole game is reading what's in your hand and what's on top of the pile.

questions.question: What's the goal in this game?
options: Empty your hand before others do.

questions.feedback_wrong: The race is to empty your hand before others empty theirs.

questions.question: Why are wild cards valuable?
options: They can be played any turn — they break out of stuck situations.
They can be saved for later games.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Wilds save you when you have nothing matching the discard pile.
questions.feedback_wrong: Wilds are insurance — when nothing else matches, they always do. Saving them for the right moment matters.

questions.question: What kind of game-design mechanic is this?
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The whole game is the cards in your hand and what to play when.
questions.feedback_wrong: Hand management: deciding what to play and what to hold from your hand.

questions.question: If you wanted players to feel STRATEGIC, which change would you try?
options: Show all hands openly so players see what others can play.
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. Open hands turn luck into planning; more wilds give more ways out. Talk about what each would change.

questions.question: Why is the no-talking rule the central element?
options: The constraint creates the puzzle — finding ways to communicate without words is the game.
The rule is just for politeness.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The constraint IS the game. Take it away and you have nothing left to play.
questions.feedback_wrong: The constraint creates the puzzle. Without the no-talking rule, charades is just guessing.

questions.question: Why is this a cooperative game (within each team)?
options: Players pass cards to each other.
The whole team works together — actor and guessers — to score the point.
Players take turns being the rule-keeper.
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Within a team, everyone is on the same side — the actor signals, the guessers decode.
questions.feedback_wrong: Within each team, players cooperate. The actor sends signals; the guessers receive them. Both win or lose together.

questions.question: What kind of game-design mechanic is this?
questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Within teams: cooperation. Across teams: competition. The communication restriction is what makes the game.
questions.feedback_wrong: It's cooperative within a team, with a strong communication restriction (no words). That restriction makes the game.

questions.question: If you wanted players to feel CREATIVE, which change would you try?
options: Show what to act out openly.
Tighten the constraint — fewer ways to communicate forces invention.
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. A tighter limit pushes players to invent; a longer timer gives them room. Talk about which you would try.
